extracted.intended_audience: general readers of classic literature / Project Gutenberg readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of a public-domain edition of Miguel de Cervantes' Don Quixote (English translation) — narrative chapters and embedded critical commentary on books of chivalry. The page is a chunk of the novel aimed at general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books of chivalry are mischievous to the State
rubrics_metrics.description: The canon: 'I for my part consider what they call books of chivalry to be mischievous to the State.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page presents a normative claim that chivalric books have harmful social effects; used as an evaluative standard that such works can be judged on their broader social/political consequences rather than merely on entertainment value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction should resemble truth (verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Fiction is all the better the more it looks like truth, and gives the more pleasure the more probability and possibility there is about it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works of fiction should aim for plausibility: inventiveness is permitted, but the reader's suspension of disbelief depends on internal probability. Authors should craft events so they seem possible within the story-world; implausible events reduce enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty and harmony / proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The enjoyment the mind feels must come from the beauty and harmony which it perceives... and nothing that has any ugliness or disproportion about it can give any pleasure.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic criteria: scenes, characters, and events should maintain proportion and harmony. Avoid grotesque or disproportionate combinations that jar the reader's aesthetic sense — such ugliness undermines pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wildly implausible scale or miraculous single-handed victories
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of episodes where 'a million of combatants' face a single hero who wins by his 'single might' — such exaggerations are unbelievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not inflate scales or outcomes to the point that they violate plausibility; narrative claims about numbers, scope, and the hero's solitary triumphs should be credible or adequately justified within the fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character behaviour must be psychologically/probably motivated
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘What shall we say of the facility with which a born queen or empress will give herself over into the arms of some unknown wandering knight?’ — i.e., characters should act in ways consistent with rank, temperament, and believable motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid improbable or gratuitous romantic/social decisions by characters that conflict with their established status or plausibility; ensure actions follow believable incentives and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid geographic/temporal impossibilities (maintain logistical plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of images like 'a great tower full of knights sails away across the sea... to-night in Lombardy and to-morrow morning in the land of Prester John' as impossible and jarring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent spatial/temporal logic. Fantastic travel or instant translocations require sufficient framework or explanation; otherwise they break verisimilitude and reduce reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction should both amuse and instruct (prefer instruction with amusement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between Milesian tales 'that aim solely at giving amusement' and apologue fables 'which amuse and instruct at the same time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that combine entertainment with moral or intellectual instruction. Solely frivolous tales may be less valuable; a balance of delight and edification is presented as superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-constructed plot: coherence among beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Plots in fiction should be wedded to the understanding of the reader... reconciling impossibilities... so that wonder and delight joined may keep pace one with the other.’ And: 'I have never yet seen any book of chivalry that puts together a connected plot complete in all its numbers, so that the middle agrees with the beginning, and the end with the beginning and middle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require structural unity and internal consistency: the plot should resolve and echo earlier elements, smooth or explain apparent impossibilities, keep the reader's understanding engaged, and balance surprise with plausibility. Avoid assembling a story as a disjointed 'chimera' of episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assembling plots as a monstrous collection of disconnected parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that some books 'construct them with such a multitude of members that it seems as though they meant to produce a chimera or monster rather than a well-proportioned figure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives should integrate episodes into a coherent whole rather than piling unrelated adventures. Each part should serve the overall design and maintain proportionality to avoid a sense of monstrous excess.
